courses.blurb: Switching converters from first principles: devices, DC–DC converters, snubbers and design.

lectures.title: Introduction and power semiconductor switches
lectures.summary: Why switch-mode conversion, ideal vs real switches, diodes, MOSFETs, IGBTs and SiC devices.
lectures.notes:
# Why switch-mode?
A linear regulator drops the excess voltage across a transistor, so its efficiency can never exceed \( V_o/V_{in} \). A switch-mode converter uses switches that are either fully on or fully off, so ideally no power is lost in them.

> An ideal switch has zero voltage when on, zero current when off, and switches instantly. Real devices lose energy in conduction and during each transition.

# Conduction and switching loss
$$P_{cond} = I_{rms}^2 \, R_{DS(on)}$$
$$P_{sw} \approx \tfrac{1}{2} V_{DS} I_D \left(t_r + t_f\right) f_s$$
Switching loss grows linearly with switching frequency, which is why soft switching (ZVS / ZCS) matters at high frequency.

lectures.title: Buck converter: steady-state analysis
lectures.summary: Volt-second balance, conversion ratio, inductor ripple and output-voltage ripple.
lectures.notes: # Volt-second balance In steady state the average inductor voltage over one switching period is zero. With duty ratio \(D\): $$\langle v_L \rangle = D\,(V_{in} - V_o) + (1-D)(-V_o) = 0$$ $$\Rightarrow \quad V_o = D\,V_{in}$$ # Inductor current ripple During the on-time the inductor sees \(V_{in}-V_o\), so its current rises linearly: $$\Delta i_L = \frac{(V_{in}-V_o)\,D}{L\,f_s} = \frac{V_o\,(1-D)}{L\,f_s}$$ # Output voltage ripple The ripple current flows into the capacitor; integrating the charge over half a period gives $$\Delta v_o = \frac{\Delta i_L}{8\,C\,f_s}$$ > **Design check:** choose \(L\) for a ripple of about 20–40% of the load current, then choose \(C\) for the allowed \(\Delta v_o\).

lectures.title: Snubber circuits: RCD turn-off snubber
lectures.summary: Why snubbers, the RCD turn-off snubber, choosing the capacitor and resistor, and snubber loss.
lectures.notes:
# Purpose
At turn-off the switch voltage rises while current is still flowing, so the switch carries high power. An RCD snubber diverts the current into a capacitor, slowing the voltage rise.

# Choosing the capacitor
If the current falls linearly in time \(t_f\) and the capacitor should reach the full voltage \(V_d\) just as the current reaches zero:
$$C_s = \frac{I_o \, t_f}{2\,V_d}$$

# Choosing the resistor
The capacitor must discharge through \(R_s\) during the minimum on-time. Allowing about \(2.3\,R_sC_s\) (discharge to 10%):
$$R_s \le \frac{t_{on,min}}{2.3\,C_s}$$

# Snubber loss
$$P_{R} = \tfrac{1}{2}\, C_s V_d^2 \, f_s$$

> A larger \(C_s\) lowers turn-off loss in the switch but raises the loss in \(R_s\). The best value balances the two.

lectures.title: DAB converter and single phase shift (SPS)
lectures.summary: Operating principle, power transfer equation and the role of the series inductance.
lectures.notes:
# Power transfer under SPS
With both bridges producing square waves shifted by \(\varphi\) (radians), the transferred power is
$$P = \frac{n\,V_1 V_2}{2\pi f_s L}\;\varphi\left(1 - \frac{|\varphi|}{\pi}\right)$$
Maximum power occurs at \(\varphi = \pi/2\). The direction of power flow follows the sign of \(\varphi\).

> The series inductance \(L\) sets the power capability: a smaller \(L\) transfers more power at the same phase shift but raises the peak current.

lectures.title: From DAB to TAB: three-port power flow
lectures.summary: Three-winding transformer, the delta-equivalent model and coupled power flow between ports.
lectures.notes:
# Delta-equivalent model
A TAB can be modelled as three bridges connected through an equivalent delta of inductances \(L_{12}, L_{13}, L_{23}\). Each link behaves like a DAB:
$$P_{ij} = \frac{V_i V_j}{2\pi f_s L_{ij}}\;\varphi_{ij}\left(1 - \frac{|\varphi_{ij}|}{\pi}\right)$$
The power at a port is the sum over its two links, e.g. \(P_1 = P_{12} + P_{13}\). Because the links share phase shifts, changing one port's power disturbs the others: this is the cross-coupling that decoupled control must handle.

blog.title: Why phase shift controls power in a dual active bridge
blog.summary: A short, visual explanation of how the phase shift between two square waves moves power across an inductor.
blog.body:
A dual active bridge has two full bridges, one on each side of a high-frequency transformer. Each bridge produces a square wave. The only thing that separates them is a series inductance \(L\).

# The key idea
If both square waves are identical and in phase, the inductor sees no voltage and no current flows. Shift one wave by an angle \(\varphi\), and a voltage appears across the inductor for part of every half-cycle. That drives current, and with it, power.

$$P = \frac{n\,V_1 V_2}{2\pi f_s L}\;\varphi\left(1 - \frac{|\varphi|}{\pi}\right)$$

# What the equation tells us
- Power flows from the leading bridge to the lagging one.
- It peaks at \(\varphi = \pi/2\).
- A smaller \(L\) gives more power for the same shift, but higher peak current.

> In a triple active bridge the same idea applies to every pair of ports, which is why the phase shifts are coupled.
